body.text: No propaganda wall can block Russians from feeling the impact of the Ukraine war in their everyday lives (Kremlin.ru)
The regime will win Russia’s election easily – the risk is winning by too much.

But no propaganda wall can block Russians from feeling the impact of the Ukraine war in their everyday lives. Seven out of ten petrol stations had run out of fuel in August and there were bowser queues in Moscow for the first time, a consequence of long-range Ukrainian drone strikes hitting oil refineries . Ukrainian drones have also attacked the Russian equivalent of Amazon, Wildberries’ warehouses .

Living standards are falling , inflation is rising, real wages are shrinking and interest rates are at 14% . The Carnegie Russia Eurasia Centre colourfully summed up the economic challenges : “Russia’s economy has operated like a marathoner on fiscal steroids – and now those steroids are wearing off”.

Russians are withdrawing billions in cash from banks amid fears private savings could be channelled into the war effort , according to The Washington Post . Opinion polls also show increased war fatigue, with support for the conflict in Ukraine having dropped from 78% in July 2025 to 66% in July this year.

While it is a given that Putin’s United Russia Party will claim the most seats, the Kremlin appears nervous. It knows that a landslide victory would be seen to be out of step with public sentiment and a sign of weakness. The ultimate margin needs to be carefully calibrated.

The party, which presently has around 70% of MPs in the 450-seat State Duma, is reportedly downgrading expectations of its share of votes and overall turnout . Kremlin officials had also reportedly discussed delaying or cancelling the vote .
Poll aggregator Politpro shows the United Russia Party is on 46% of the vote, with a -3.8% swing.

Putin, who is notoriously worried about assassination attempts and rarely leaves Moscow, has been forced to hit the campaign hustings to conduct a listening tour over the summer months. Magically, wherever Putin went, petrol prices fell .

Things also got spicy when Russia’s Supreme Court last month banned the only anti-war opposition party, Yabloko, from running. Previously, Yabloko was tolerated within the system as a “constructive opposition” to provide some sheen of democratic legitimacy . Protest votes may instead flow elsewhere to other smaller parties like the Communists or New People.

“They are so afraid of everything right now that they even removed Yabloko from the election,” Yulia Navalnaya, the widow of slain Russian opposition leader Alexei Navalny, said, urging Russians not to lose hope .
“Vote for any party except United Russia.”
The Kremlin knows that a landslide victory would be seen to be out of step with public sentiment and a sign of weakness.

Before it was sidelined, Yabloko, one of Russia’s oldest active parties, had been steadily gaining social media traction with young people, who are fretting over a potential new round of troop mobilisation.
“As of today, there is no scenario that would require a mobilisation,” Putin said in carefully nuanced comments earlier this month .
But the groundwork is being prepared , some analysts believe.

Anecdotally, young Russian men are fleeing abroad, but the exodus is not as large as in 2022 . The Kremlin’s “meat grinder” war tactics are sending Russian sons to their deaths in the Ukraine “kill zone” at an extraordinary rate. Recent British figures estimate more than half a million Russian troops have been killed in battle in Ukraine, part of 1.5 million casualties. According to the Center for Strategic and International Studies , Russian fatalities in Ukraine are more than four times greater than all US fatalities in all wars combined since the Second World War, and more than nine times greater than all Soviet and Russian fatalities in all wars combined since 1945.
Things have to be pretty grim if the Kremlin is sending 14th-century bones to lift morale on the front line.

No matter how Russians vote in the 18–20 September election, the foreign policy outlook and war trajectory will be more of the same. Putin is unlikely to be suddenly won over by flailing US diplomacy . So long as the 73-year-old strongman remains at the apex of power in Moscow, the war in Ukraine will grind on.
Old mate is not ruling out sticking around until 2036 .
